samples.summary: `READ_GATED_METHODS` authorizes `AttachDocument` as a read, so a share-link `viewer` can write via the change pack carried in the attach RPC — repeatably, because `DetachDocument` is unconditionally allowed
samples.evidence:
`READ_GATED_METHODS = new Set(['AttachDocument'])` (line 108) makes `checkAttribute` compute `needWrite = attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)` (line 334), i.e. `false` for attach. `hasAccess` then returns `true` for a viewer link whose `documentId` matches (line 370: `needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`).

Attacker path: a visitor holding a viewer-role share link POSTs it to the public `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` (auth.controller.ts:82) to mint a Yorkie token, takes the project public key out of any visitor's bundle, and drives a hand-rolled `@yorkie-js/sdk` client. They build a local `Document`, apply arbitrary local changes, then `attach` — the SDK sends those local changes in the attach ChangePack, and the webhook is asked to authorize the attach only as a read, so it allows. `DetachDocument` is short-circuited to ALLOW before any token check (line 221-223), so the write/detach/re-attach loop is unbounded. That the attach pack is really applied is asserted by this branch's own material: `docs/tasks/active/20260907-notes-share-toolbar-lessons.md` explains that `initialRoot`/`initialPresence` seeds ride the attach pack and are therefore refused as a `rw` `PushPull`, which is the entire motivation for the `initialRoot={readOnly ? {} : ...}` fixes in this diff.

Net effect: on the very deployments this PR switches to enforce-by-default, "viewer means read-only" is enforced only against clients that put their changes in `PushPull`. The residual is documented (`docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md` § Risks) and deliberately accepted, but it is still a bypass of the only server-side gate on a viewer's write, and features are being layered on top of it (`assertYorkieAuthEnforced` for the public template gallery).

samples.summary: An unscoped `yorkie-service` token is a deployment-wide, unrevocable read/write credential that `decideService` blanket-allows, and the ops scripts transmit exactly that token to a Yorkie server (in the copy script, to a second deployment's server)
samples.evidence:
`decideService` returns `ALLOW` for any method and any document when the payload carries no `key` (lines 289-291). `copy-yorkie-documents.ts:53` and the two migrate scripts (`migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221`, `migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347`) call `yorkieServiceTokenInjector(secret)` / `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv()` with no `key`, so those tokens authorize read/write on *every* document of the deployment that minted them.

The token does not stay in-process: the SDK sends it to whatever `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR`/`--*-rpc-addr` names, on every RPC, and Yorkie echoes it into the webhook body. So anything that can observe it — a plaintext (`http://`) RPC hop, Yorkie server logs, a hosted/third-party Yorkie, or the *other* deployment's operator in the copy case — holds a full read/write credential for the whole deployment for `YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN` (operator-settable; `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv` passes `process.env.YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN` straight through, so a deployment that set a long lifetime for user tokens extends this one too). There is no revocation short of rotating `JWT_SECRET`, which invalidates every session. `signYorkieServiceToken` also carries no method restriction, so such a token is accepted for `RestoreRevision`/`GetRevision` on any document as well.

The per-document scoping added for `YorkieService.withDocument` is the right shape; the ops-script exception is where the blast radius lives and it is granted by omission of a claim rather than by an explicit, narrower credential.

samples.summary: The service token is signed with the session-signing `JWT_SECRET` and carries no `aud`/`iss`, although it is deliberately handed to an external component (the Yorkie server, possibly third-party); only claim-name discrimination keeps the token families apart
samples.evidence:
`signYorkieServiceToken` (line 61-70) signs `{ typ, key? }` with the caller's secret, which in every production path is `JWT_SECRET` — the same key `AuthService.createTokens` uses for session access tokens (auth.service.ts:58,121) and, when `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET` is unset, for refresh tokens too (auth.service.ts:59-60). No `audience`/`issuer` is set or verified anywhere (`verifyYorkieToken` passes only `{ secret }`, auth.service.ts:96).

Today the families are separated only by claim discrimination: `JwtStrategy.validate` requires `tokenType === 'access'` (jwt.strategy.ts:36) and `verifyYorkieToken` requires one of three `typ` values, so I could not find a live cross-use. The weakness is structural: this is the first token minted *for an external party* under the session key, and any future verifier that checks the signature without re-checking the discriminator would accept a credential that a Yorkie server (or its logs) already holds. A distinct signing secret, or an `aud: 'yorkie-webhook'` asserted on both sides, would make the boundary explicit rather than conventional.

samples.summary: `decideService` ignores the verb entirely, so a request-path service token authorizes writes on its document even for the server paths that attach `syncMode: 'readonly'`
samples.evidence: The scoped branch compares only `attr.key !== identity.key` (lines 306-314) and never looks at `attr.verb`, so a token minted for a read-only server path — e.g. `ApiV1CellsController.getCells`, which passes `{ syncMode: 'readonly' }` (cells.controller.ts:112) and mints its token through the same `yorkieServiceTokenInjector(this.tokenSecret, this.tokenExpiresIn, docKey)` in yorkie.service.ts:83 — is worth read *and* write on that document key for its lifetime. The payload has no field expressing the intended verb (`YorkieServiceTokenPayload` is `{ typ, key? }`, yorkie-service-token.ts:33-55). Carrying the intended access level in the claim and enforcing it here would make a leaked read-path token worth only a read.

samples.summary: The copy script argues (in its new comment) that secrets must not be on argv, while still taking the Postgres URL, Mongo URL and Yorkie API key on argv — and interpolates operator-controlled values into a `mongosh --eval` script
samples.evidence:
`sideTokenInjector`'s new doc comment (lines 31-33) states that "a secret on the command line is readable by any local process through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and is echoed into shell history and CI logs" — yet `--database-url` (line 92), `--mongo-url` (line 97) and `--source-api-key` (line 108) are still parsed from argv and carry credentials of exactly that kind, and `mongoUrl` is additionally passed as an `execFileSync('mongosh', [...])` argument (line 203), making it visible in that child's cmdline too. The reasoning added for the JWT secrets applies verbatim to these three.

Separately, `fetchExistingYorkieKeys` builds a JavaScript program by string interpolation and hands it to `mongosh --eval` (lines 186-207). `JSON.stringify` on `projectPublicKey`/`candidateKeys` blocks the ordinary quote break-out, so I could not construct a working injection (U+2028/U+2029 are legal in ES2019+ string literals, giving at most a syntax error), and the inputs are operator-supplied `--document`/`--project-public-key` values rather than end-user data. Pre-existing code, flagged as the adjacent eval-injection surface rather than a demonstrated exploit.

samples.summary: Docs and the controller comment claim only the literal `false` selects shadow mode, but `isYorkieAuthEnforced` trims and lowercases — so `FALSE`, `False` and ` false ` also disable enforcement, a wider opt-out than documented
samples.evidence: `isYorkieAuthEnforced` returns `raw?.trim().toLowerCase() !== 'false'` (line 30). The README says "The literal `false`, and only that, selects shadow mode: log the access decision but never deny. A typo therefore enforces" (packages/backend/README.md:101-108) and self-hosting.md:185 says "Set it to `false` — and only that exact value". The controller's boot warning likewise asserts the variable "is set to false" (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:179). The spec pins the wider reading (`['FALSE', false]`, `[' false ', false]` in yorkie-auth.controller.spec.ts), so the code is intentional and the documentation is what is wrong. Direction of the discrepancy matters for a security setting: an operator who believes only exact `false` opts out may leave a `FALSE`/` false ` in a compose file and be unprotected while believing a typo fails closed.

samples.summary: Security-posture claims contradicting this PR's own default flip are left in place — including in a file this PR adds — asserting the webhook "allows everything" until `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=true` and that the client read-only wrapper is the write boundary
samples.evidence:
The file added by this diff states "the webhook allows everything until a deployment both registers its methods and sets `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=true`" (packages/notes/src/store/read-only.ts:63-64), which is false after `isYorkieAuthEnforced` makes unset mean enforce. Its sibling still says the webhook "ships in shadow mode by default" (packages/docs/src/store/read-only.ts:40), and the docs engine repeats "the Yorkie auth webhook that would be that check ships in shadow mode unless `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=true`, so in a stock deployment this is the write boundary for a viewer share token" (packages/docs/src/view/editor.ts:4413-4414). Same stale premise in packages/frontend/README.md:37, docs/design/sharing.md:208, docs/design/revision-history.md:504, docs/design/docs/docs-image-editing.md:299-302 and docs/design/template-gallery.md:668.

This is security-relevant, not cosmetic: the branch's own design notes argue at length that treating a client-side read-only mount as the access-control boundary is the mistake that let viewer write paths ship, and these comments are precisely the statements a future reviewer would rely on to make that mistake again. `docs/design/*` top-level files are link-checked but nothing checks these assertions.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as claimed. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:108 puts 'AttachDocument' in READ_GATED_METHODS; lines 332-334 therefore compute needWrite=false for attach regardless of the 'rw' verb Yorkie sends; line 370 returns true for any share-link identity (including role 'viewer') whose link.documentId matches, so a viewer's AttachDocument is authorized. DetachDocument is unconditionally ALLOWed before any token verification (lines 66, 221-223), making the attach/detach/re-attach loop unbounded. The credential is publicly obtainable: POST /auth/yorkie-token/share (auth/auth.controller.ts:82-90) has no JwtAuthGuard and mints a Yorkie token from any share token. Since AttachDocument carries a change pack and the webhook body contains no pack to inspect, nothing in this repo refuses a viewer's writes smuggled in the attach pack; only post-attach writes are refused at PushPull. The repository's own design doc concedes exactly this residual (docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:310-318) and the unit spec pins the viewer attach as allowed (yorkie-auth.controller.spec.ts:281-294), so the behavior is intentional but not guarded. This is authorization/access control (a viewer bypassing the only server-side gate on viewer writes), squarely in lane, with auth-bypass impact. Deliberate documented acceptance and 'needs an upstream truthful verb' are not refutation grounds, and pre-existing-ness is explicitly not one either, so I found no basis to drop it.

Unscoped tokens are really minted: yorkie-service-token.ts:66-70/82-91 omit `key` by default, and migrate-yorkie-cf-ranges.ts:221, migrate-yorkie-worksheet-shape.ts:347 and copy-yorkie-documents.ts:53 all mint keyless tokens that the SDK transmits to the configured Yorkie server on every RPC; yorkie-service-token.ts:104-115 forwards YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN unchanged, so a long user-token lifetime extends this credential too. finding.summary: `READ_GATED_METHODS` makes `AttachDocument` authorize as a read, so a viewer-role share link can write to the document via the attach change pack — the one write the webhook exists to refuse
finding.evidence:
`READ_GATED_METHODS = new Set(['AttachDocument'])` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:108) feeds `checkAttribute`'s `needWrite = REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)` (line 332-334). Before this change an `AttachDocument` carrying verb `rw` required `link.role === 'editor'` (hasAccess, line 370); now attach is authorized with `needWrite=false`, i.e. any identity with *read* access.

Attack: a holder of a viewer-role share token (or a public-template `previewToken`, which is `listing.shareLink.token` — template.service.ts:1314) does (1) `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` with the token to get a signed `yorkie-share` Yorkie token, (2) builds a bare `@yorkie-js/sdk` client with the project public key that ships in every visitor's bundle, (3) `new Document(key)`, `doc.update(...)` locally, then `client.attach(doc)`. The SDK sends the accumulated local change pack inside the `AttachDocument` RPC (which is precisely why the diff observes attach always carries `rw`), so the webhook is asked with `AttachDocument`/`rw`, answers ALLOW on read access, and the pack is applied server-side. `DetachDocument` is unconditionally allowed (`ALWAYS_ALLOWED_METHOD`, line 66/221 — no token needed at all), so the write loop is detach → mutate → re-attach, unbounded.

Impact: server-side enforcement of "viewer means read-only" does not exist for any non-browser client, on an enforcing deployment. It also undercuts the premise of `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` (template-review.ts:104): every anonymous visitor to a public template card holds a preview token, and an edit puts the listing back into the human-only review queue, so the gallery-drain abuse that gate was written to prevent is still reachable, only at the cost of running a script instead of one HTTP request. The change acknowledges this residual in its own comments (lines 99-106, template-review.ts:85-96) but ships the weakened gate; reporting it because the gate now reads as covered whi

verdict.reason: The claimed code is present verbatim. `READ_GATED_METHODS = new Set(['AttachDocument'])` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:108) feeds `needWrite = REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:332-334), so an `AttachDocument` carrying verb `rw` is authorized with needWrite=false and `hasAccess` returns true for a share link of role `viewer` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:370, which otherwise requires `link.role === 'editor'`). The repo's own test pins this ALLOW (yorkie-auth.controller.spec.ts:281-294). `DetachDocument` is allowed before any token check (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:66,221), enabling an unbounded detach->mutate->re-attach loop. The write path is not hypothetical per the repo itself: yorkie-auth.controller.ts:99-106 and docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:310-319 state that a hand-rolled client can smuggle a change pack in the attach and repeat it, and template-review.ts:88-100 concedes that assertYorkieAuthEnforced is 'a bound on the residual, not its removal' while still gating the anonymously-reachable public template tier (previewToken is a viewer capability, template.service.ts:142-164). No refuting ground holds: the code is present as described (not `not-present`); nothing else re-checks the attach change pack, and PushPull is a later RPC that cannot un-apply the pack already accepted at attach (not `already-guarded`); and a role check removed from the enforced path for one method is core authorization/access control, in this lens's lane, so a documented deliberate trade-off does not make it `out-of-scope`. Impact is a server-side authorization bypass of 'viewer means read-only' for any non-browser client on an enforcing deployment, which is critical under this rubric.

finding.summary: Read-only sheet mount still lets a signed-in viewer-role share-link visitor write comment threads/replies/resolutions into the CRDT root; the new YorkieStore.readOnly gate does not cover the comment mutators and no UI gate stands in front of them
finding.evidence: Vector: a visitor who has a Wafflebase account but is NOT a workspace member opens a viewer-role share link to a spreadsheet. shared-document.tsx:283 mounts SheetView readOnly={true}, so the store is new YorkieStore(doc, tabId, true) (sheet-view.tsx:1012). Selection still works in read-only, and the onSelectionChange handler at sheet-view.tsx:1128-1169 auto-opens the comment popover (setCommentPopoverOpen(true), line 1168) whenever the selected cell carries an unresolved thread - it has no readOnly check. The popover is then rendered at sheet-view.tsx:1719 with no readOnly prop, and CommentPopover.tsx:47 computes isReadOnly = currentUser === null, i.e. it only asks 'are you signed in?', never 'what is your share role?'. Because the visitor is signed in, commentAuthor is non-null (sheet-view.tsx:191) and CommentThreadCard renders the reply composer (CommentThreadCard.tsx:188) and the resolve toggle (line 107). Clicking them calls handleCommentReply / handleCommentResolve / handleCommentEdit / handleCommentDelete (sheet-view.tsx:921, 940, 967, 974), which call the RAW store: YorkieStore.addReply -> this.doc.update((root) => applyAddReply(ws, ...)) at yorkie-store.ts:1329, setThreadResolved at :1364, editComment at :1348, deleteComment at :1354. None of these consult the readOnly field this delta introduced, and sheets has no read-only store proxy (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts is the datasource query-result store, not an access wrapper), so the write reaches doc.update and the next PushPull carries verb rw. With YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE unset the webhook refuses it (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:370, needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true), so the observable damage is the viewer's sync wedging - the exact failure this delta exists to remove, just via a different write. With the documented shadow-mode rollout option (YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=false) the write PERSISTS, i.e. a viewer-role visitor mutates a document they hold read-only access to. Docs closes

verdict.reason: The finding claims the comment mutators have no readOnly gate and that no UI gate stands in front of them; both exist in the working tree. YorkieStore.assertWritable (yorkie-store.ts:1310-1314) throws when the store was constructed read-only, and it is the first statement of addThread (:1321), addReply (:1347), editComment (:1367), deleteComment (:1375) and setThreadResolved (:1386) — so no comment write reaches doc.update() on a read-only mount regardless of caller. On the UI side, CommentPopover accepts a readOnly prop (CommentPopover.tsx:32,54) and computes isReadOnly = readOnly || currentUser === null (:56), and sheet-view.tsx:1738 passes readOnly={readOnly} at the very render site the finding says has no such prop. isReadOnly is forwarded as CommentThreadCard readOnly (:103), which hides the resolve toggle (CommentThreadCard.tsx:107) and the reply composer (:188), while the new-thread composer is gated at CommentPopover.tsx:114 with a view-only message at :123-128. The described vector (signed-in viewer-role visitor writing threads/replies/resolutions into the CRDT root) is therefore blocked at both layers.
